articles.title: AI Made Coding Cheaper. So Why Is Building Software Still So Expensive?
articles.description: I can generate a full authentication flow with a database schema, API routes, and unit tests in under...
articles.body_html:
I can generate a full authentication flow with a database schema, API routes, and unit tests in under 30 seconds.

I can refactor a messy component into clean React hooks with one prompt.

I can ask an AI to explain a complex regex, and it will break it down for me line by line.

So why did my last "simple" feature still take three weeks to reach production?

If writing code is now practically free, why does building software still feel so incredibly expensive?

The Paradox of the 30-Second Pull Request

Last month, I was working on a feature that usually takes a few days. I fired up Cursor (or your AI tool of choice), typed a detailed prompt, and watched the code materialize on my screen.

It was beautiful. Clean. Formatted.

I felt like a 10x developer. I opened a Pull Request that same afternoon, feeling incredibly proud of my "velocity."

Then the real work started.

It took my teammate two days to review it. Not because the code was wrong, but because the AI had introduced a subtle edge case in the caching logic that neither of us initially understood.

When we finally deployed it, it broke a legacy system that the AI didn't even know existed.

We spent the next week debugging, rolling back, and rewriting the "perfect" AI-generated code to fit our actual, messy production environment.

That's when the uncomfortable realization hit me:

Writing the code was never the expensive part. It was always the cheapest part.

The Jevons Paradox in Software Engineering

In economics, there's a concept called the Jevons Paradox. It states that as technological progress increases the efficiency with which a resource is used, total consumption of that resource may actually increase, rather than decrease.

AI made writing code cheap. So what happened? We just demanded more code.

When it took a week to write a feature, we shipped one feature. Now that it takes an hour to write the code, management asks for five features in the same week.

But the bottleneck of software engineering was never typing speed. It's not the syntax. It's the cognitive load of context.

AI doesn't know your company's three-year-old architectural decisions. It doesn't know why that one microservice is fragile. It doesn't know the business logic that lives in the head of the developer who left the company two years ago.

So where did the cost go? It shifted to three places we rarely measure:

1. The Review and Trust Tax

Reading code is vastly harder than writing it. When a human writes code, you can ask them, "Why did you do it this way?" When AI writes code, you have to reverse-engineer its logic just to trust it. We are now spending more time reviewing code than we ever did writing it.

2. The Context Debt

AI is a brilliant sprinter, but a terrible architect. It can build a function perfectly, but it doesn't understand how that function breaks the other 50,000 lines of code in your repository. The "integration cost" of AI code is astronomically high.

3. The Maintenance Bill

Generating code is cheap. Maintaining generative code is expensive. AI often writes code that is technically correct but idiomatically weird. It creates abstractions that don't make sense to humans. And six months from now, someone is going to have to read it.

How We Actually Fix This

If code is cheap, we have to stop optimizing for typing speed. We have to start optimizing for decision-making.

1. Move the bottleneck to design.
Don't prompt AI to "build this feature." Prompt it to "suggest three architectural approaches." Spend the saved time deciding which approach is best for your specific context.

2. Protect your review capacity.
Your senior developers are now bottlenecks. If an AI generates 1,000 lines of code, the senior developer's brain is the only thing standing between that code and production. Buy them more time for review.

3. Focus on "Delete" over "Write".
The best use of AI is not to add new code, but to delete old code. Use it to untangle messes, write missing tests, and refactor legacy systems. Use the speed to reduce your maintenance burden.

The uncomfortable truth

AI didn't make software engineering easier.

It just changed the job from "writing code" to "editing code."

And editing requires a deeper understanding of the system than writing ever did.

If you don't understand the code an AI generated for you, you don't own that code. The code owns you. And the debt you are accumulating is going to come due.

Writing code is now a commodity. Understanding what to build, how it fits into the big picture, and how to keep it secure is where the real value lies.

You don't need to be a faster coder anymore. You need to be a better systems thinker.

Now I'm curious, because I know I'm not the only one feeling this shift.

Have you noticed that AI has made you type faster, but your features still take just as long to ship? Where is the biggest bottleneck on your team right now?

Is it the reviews? The testing? The architecture?

Drop it in the comments below. Let's figure out what the new "10x developer" actually looks like.

articles.title: Certificate authority keys: eMudhra's browser and runtime trust gap
articles.description: The eMudhra certificate authority incident shows why browser blocklists and runtime CA bundles need separate checks in deployed applications.
articles.body_html:
The eMudhra certificate authority incident has an awkward developer-facing cleanup problem. Browser vendors can block a compromised certificate chain while a deployed application keeps reading an older CA bundle. Eight intermediate signing keys were compromised, and your browser's update history cannot tell you which trust material a containerized service has loaded. The place to close the incident is the deployed client's actual validation path.

TL;DR

  • Mozilla's incident report identifies eight compromised intermediate signing keys: six for TLS and two for code signing. A compromised intermediate key gives its holder signing authority under that certificate.
  • Mozilla independently recovered the affected keys. The public report describes flawed key generation and says the certificates date to April 2025. Actual misuse against other clients remains unknown.
  • The report describes no certificate transparency entries for those intermediates during the period. Its browser-exploitation conclusion is scoped to clients enforcing certificate transparency.
  • Browser blocking, CA revocation and application trust-store updates are separate mechanisms. Check the CA bundle and validation configuration used by the running application.
  • Primary release evidence confirms certifi 2026.10.19 and Node 24.22.1 for the branch discussed in the episode. A custom trust bundle or another release branch needs its own check.

What happened to the certificate authority keys?

The public incident page was published on October 20. It says the original reporter, Wayne, demonstrated control of eight intermediate CA private keys by signing a fixed message with each one. The message was “We have a problem here - Wayne”. The root-program teams received the report on October 17.

Mozilla's initial incident description provides independent confirmation. Mozilla verified the proof of key control and independently recovered the impacted keys without knowing Wayne's method. The report now says the keys were generated incorrectly and could be recovered from the certificates.

That supports a specific conclusion: the signing keys were recoverable, and outsiders demonstrated control. It gives us no basis to invent a separate server break-in, an attacker list or a set of affected customer accounts. The incident page says actual misuse against clients outside the browser ecosystem remains unknown. Urgency can coexist with an honest account of what the evidence establishes.

The eight-key figure also needs its categories. Mozilla identifies six TLS intermediates and two code-signing intermediates. The episode focuses on the TLS-client cleanup; those two categories do different jobs. The number is a count of compromised intermediate signing keys. Root certificates sit at a different layer of a client's trust decision.

How an intermediate CA fits into TLS validation

A TLS server presents a certificate chain. A simplified view has the server certificate, an intermediate certificate and a root that the client recognizes as trusted. Real deployments can include more intermediate levels and cross-signs. The client follows the presented chain and applies its validation rules, including the trust material available in its own environment.

The intermediate's private key authorizes signatures under that intermediate certificate. Someone controlling that key can create a mathematically valid signature. The usefulness of the signature depends on the client's trust in the signer and on the other checks that the client performs.

This explains why certificate verification has several moving parts. Chain building and cryptographic verification establish relationships between certificates. Trust policy decides which authorities the client accepts. Revocation or specific distrust information can withdraw acceptance after a problem is discovered. Certificate transparency adds another requirement in clients that enforce it.

Those checks have different inputs and different update paths. A root bundle can be current for ordinary chain building while an intermediate-specific blocking rule arrives through a browser's emergency distribution mechanism. Another program can have a bundled store with a different maintenance schedule. Treating the word “trust” as one global switch hides the work your application actually performs.

What certificate transparency tells us about exposure

The public incident report dates the affected certificates to April 2025. It reports no certificate transparency entries for those intermediates during the period and concludes that CT-enforcing clients such as the named major browsers could not have been attacked through this route.

That qualification belongs next to the alarming headline. A demonstrated ability to sign certificates under an intermediate is evidence of compromised authority. A successful impersonation also depends on the client's rules. For a browser enforcing transparency, a forged chain would have to satisfy that additional requirement.

The same incident page points out that many other clients do not enforce certificate transparency. It leaves actual exploitation against those clients unknown. I would keep those two statements together in an incident ticket: the extra browser requirement narrows the exposure claim; other clients require their own assessment.

This article relies on the report and Mozilla's confirmation. I have not independently surveyed CT logs, recovered a private key or tested every client mentioned here. There is no exploit demonstration in the episode. The distinction matters because a source's scoped conclusion can turn into a much broader claim when somebody abbreviates it for a dashboard.

Certificate revocation and the runtime trust-store gap

The report records Firefox and Chrome blocking action on October 17, Apple action on October 19 and Microsoft action on October 20. It also says the CA revoked the compromised intermediates. Other clients can require software updates because they do not consume the revocation information needed to reject those chains.

Publishing a revocation changes the information available to validators. It helps a client only when that client receives and applies the information. A program that validates against a static bundle needs a mitigation compatible with its actual validation mechanism.

Mozilla's incident thread describes emergency removal of trust in emSign ECC Root CA - G3 after discussion with downstream maintainers. That protects clients which lack revocation handling or a mechanism to withdraw trust in a specific intermediate. Removing a root from a store changes the acceptance of a chain; it does not, by itself, establish compromise of that root's private key.

Even browser delivery needed checking. In comment 29, Mozilla says some Android profiles were failing to apply the updated blocklist at startup. It reports a fix shipped in Firefox 158.0.2. Vendor remediation dates describe vendor actions. Your phone still has an installed version and local state, which is why keeping the browser current remains part of the advice.

What certifi and Node actually released

For Python software using certifi, the 2026.10.19 release gives a concrete maintained package to inspect. Its release commit is titled “Restore unaffected emSign roots (#439) (#440)”. The diff restores unaffected roots after an earlier removal.

That correction is useful operational evidence. Maintainers are trying to reject the dangerous chain while preserving legitimate services. A blanket instruction to delete every certificate carrying an eMudhra or emSign name would discard the distinctions recorded in the release history. Use the maintained update appropriate to the actual dependency and configuration.

For Node, 24.22.1 shipped on October 21 as a security release. Its notable changes include “crypto: update root certificates to NSS 3.131.1”. The linked root-update PR is the primary implementation evidence for the bundled-root change.

That is a verified release for the Node branch named here. It is not an inventory of every Node process you operate. Other branches need their own release advice, and a process using a custom or system CA configuration needs that configuration examined. Likewise, updating one Python environment cannot establish the dependency state of every virtual environment or container image.

Check the deployed process, then test the right thing

I would begin with the application that makes the connection. Identify the running environment and the trust material it actually uses. Record whether it relies on an operating-system store, a runtime bundle, a dependency such as certifi or a custom CA file. This is investigation guidance, rather than a claim that one configuration applies to every framework.

Apply the relevant maintained update, rebuild the deployment when the bundle is baked into an image, and restart processes where they need to load changed trust material. Verify the deployed state afterwards. An updated workstation and an old production container can happily coexist while making different certificate decisions.

The public incident page supplies test hosts and offline chains for checking clients. Keep certificate-validation failures separate from transport failures. A network timeout can come from routing, DNS, a proxy or an unavailable host. It does not prove that a validator rejected the compromised intermediate. The page diagnostic in the research browser included timeouts, so the episode makes no experimental “this browser is safe” claim from that observation.

Preserve certificate verification while following the maintainers' documented checks. A successful investigation should leave you with the client's real environment, its trust configuration and a meaningful validation result. “The browser update installed” leaves the server-side question unanswered.

Also in this episode: Tor and an SSH identity warning

A researcher account published October 20 describes 333 compromised Tor exit relays and an earlier-October SSH interception campaign. Its roughly ten-percent figure counts relays with different capacities. It does not measure intercepted traffic share. A Tor network-health operator notice confirms reports of SSH interception on compromised hosts. The researcher noticed a changed server-identity warning. Verify such a change through a trusted channel before accepting it and logging in. Routing and endpoint authentication have separate jobs.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I stamped the eMudhra story NEEDS REVIEW because I want the deployed client's trust checked before the incident gets closed. Browser remediation is useful evidence for that browser. The application owns another validation decision, and somebody needs to verify it.

FAQ

Were eight root private keys compromised?

Mozilla identifies eight intermediate signing keys, with six TLS intermediates and two code-signing intermediates. Emergency root distrust is a mitigation decision at a different layer.

Does updating Chrome update certifi inside my container?

A separately bundled application dependency has its own deployment path. Inspect the running environment and the bundle the client actually uses.

Does a failed connection prove the chain is blocked?

A certificate-validation error is meaningful for that check. A timeout alone leaves the certificate decision unobserved.

Was the Tor incident happening when the article was published?

The researcher describes interception beginning October 2 and relays flagged or shut down over the following days. The write-up was published October 20.

Sources

  • Public eMudhra incident report
  • Mozilla incident 2083449
  • certifi 2026.10.19 release
  • certifi restoration commit
  • Node 24.22.1 security release
  • Node root-certificate update PR
  • KABA's Tor researcher report
  • Tor operator notice

articles.title: When Your Agent Refuses to Collaborate: Why Propositional Logic and Basic Hygiene Beat Raw Vibe Coding
articles.description: Spending hours debugging AI-generated code with more AI? The problem isn't the model—it's a lack of...
articles.body_html:
Spending hours debugging AI-generated code with more AI? The problem isn't the model—it's a lack of domain architecture, propositional logic, and agent-native repository guardrails.

I keep seeing the same complaint across X, Reddit, and Dev.to: developers spending six hours debugging code that took an AI assistant ten minutes to generate—usually by throwing more prompts at the exact same assistant until the codebase collapses into an unmaintainable hallucination loop.

When your agent "refuses to collaborate," the problem usually isn't the model, but I think most of the time, it comes down to one of two things (or both): a lack of propositional logic in how we formulate instructions, and an absence of basic software engineering hygiene adapted for the AI era.

Basically, if you treat an LLM like a magic 8-ball, you get magic 8-ball architecture, and you can't act surprised. Here is why domain expertise still rules, and the exact stack I use to stop arguing with my agents and make them ship production-grade code on the first pass.

1. Propositional Logic vs. "Make Me Money, Bro"

Prompt engineering isn't about knowing secret buzzwords, but applied propositional logic. You cannot formalize a system if you don't understand the premises, constraints, and state transitions of the thing you are building.

A good friend of mine, who's actually a solid developer with a decade of experience in crypto spent months trying to build a trading bot using AI assistants. Every attempt ended in broken execution loops, bad math, or hallucinated SDK methods.

I asked him what he actually prompted the agent to do.
His answer: "Just make me f*cking trading bot that makes money, bro."

With no comments on his prompt, I took his failure as a personal challenge, sitting down with the exact same class of model, but instead of asking for "a bot that makes money," I gave it deterministic architectural constraints:

  • Routing & Execution: Target Uniswap V2 router contracts specifically for liquidity pools.
  • Chain Indexing: Parse transaction hashes and state logs via Etherscan and Basescan APIs.
  • Oracle / Pricing Layer: Pull real-time price conversions and slippage baselines through the CoinGecko API.
  • Security & Pre-Flight Checks: Integrate Skillware's wallet screening and contract reader microservices to verify token contracts and prevent honeypot execution before signing any transaction.

and much more. From sentiment analysis pulled form the web, to technical analysis and output formatting.

The agent delivered a working, modular trading bot in less than a few hours.

Why This Gatekeeping Should Exist

If you want to build a nuclear reactor, you need a working grasp of nuclear physics, material sciences, and thermodynamics, and if you are a hairdresser trying to vibe-code a nuclear reactor in your garage, you are going to fail—and honestly, for the better.

This is a form of natural gatekeeping I fully support, as in the AI era, raw syntax memorization is cheap, which makes taste, deep industry expertise, cross-domain knowledge, and architectural intuition more valuable than ever. "I have a cool idea, let's vibe-code it" hits a brick wall the second your system encounters real-world entropy.

2. Treat Day Zero as Production-Grade

The fastest way to eliminate back-and-forth prompting is to stop treating AI prototypes like scratchpads. From the very first commit, set up your repository as if it’s going to production tomorrow:

  • Strict Git Versioning & Changelogs: Force atomic commits and maintain a living CHANGELOG.md following Keep a Changelog standards.
  • Automated Testing & Edge-Case Simulations: Unit tests aren't enough. Build stress tests and simulation scripts that throw malformed payloads, rate limits, and network drops at your code.
  • Linters, Formatters & CI Gates: Wire up ruff, eslint, prettier, or strict type-checking (mypy/tsc) inside local pre-commit hooks and GitHub Actions.

When these hard gates exist in the repo, the agent doesn't have to guess whether its code works—the environment tells it immediately.

3. Write an Agent-Native CONTRIBUTING.md

Historically, CONTRIBUTING.md was written for humans: "Please be nice in the issues, follow our code of conduct, and use this PR template."

Look at your commit history today, and think who is actually writing the bulk of the boilerplate and patches? AI agents. Your documentation should target the entities doing the heavy lifting, not humans that copy paste contributing guides and feed them straight up to their assistants without even reading them.

In all my repos, I include an AI-Native Contributing Guide or Workflow (you can use it alongside files like AGENTS.md or .cursorrules if that's your cup of tea) that speaks directly to autonomous and/or semi-autonomous logical systems, employed as coding agents in cold, unambiguous operational logic:

What Goes Into an Agent-Native Guide:

  1. The Mandatory Execution Loop: Define the exact workflow from Iteration -> Local Verification -> Test Suite Execution -> Changelog Update -> Commit. The agent is forbidden from asking for human review until all verification gates pass with zero warnings.
  2. Ripple Effects & Hidden Dependencies: Agents struggle with implicit coupling across files. Map it out explicitly:
    • "If you bump the version in pyproject.toml, you MUST also update __version__ in src/__init__.py and append an entry to CHANGELOG.md."
    • "If you modify scripts/ingest.py, you must update its mock fixtures in tests/test_ingest.py and sync the CLI flags in README.md."
  3. State & Memory Anchors: Instruct the agent to read CHANGELOG.md and recent git log -n 5 outputs before proposing changes. This gives the agent instant episodic memory of what has already been tried, what was recently refactored, and what is next on the roadmap. 
<!-- Example snippet from an AI-Native CONTRIBUTING.md -->
## Agent Operational Protocol
1. READ `CHANGELOG.md` and run `pytest` before writing any code to establish baseline health.
2. COUPLED FILES: Any schema modification in `core/models.py` requires an immediate sync in `api/validators.py` and `docs/schema.md`.
3. HARD GATE: Do not return control to the human operator until `make lint && make test && make simulate` exits with code 0.

4. Better Diffs, Less Micromanagement

Setting up this stack does two things simultaneously:

First, for experienced engineers, it kills micromanagement. You literally stop acting as a human linter copy-pasting stack traces back into a chat window, giving the agent a sandboxed environment with strict physics, and it iterates until it satisfies the compiler and test suite.

Second, for AI-native builders with minimal software backgrounds, this structure is how you actually learn. When you have clean changelogs, updated docs, and atomic git diffs, you stop blindly accepting 500-line code dumps you don't understand. You can look at a commit and ask sharp, architectural questions:

"Why did you modify the state handler in this diff instead of the retry wrapper?"

Over time, you start recognizing the behavioral patterns and blind spots of your AI assistants. You learn how to guide them with precision rather than frustration, which makes things easier for both sides.

Wrapping Up

AI assistants might repalce many things according to narrative intensive marketing headlines, but I assure you, they aren't replacing engineering discipline, but penalizing the lack of it at 10x speed.

Know your domain. Express your requirements with logical precision. Build hard verification gates into your repositories, and write documentation for the systems actually reading your codebase.

Most importantly: be respectful to your assistants, have fun experimenting, and enjoy the craft of building things from scratch!

articles.title: 40 Bytes a Call, Just to Pass Four Ints
articles.description: A params array allocates a fresh array on every call. Switching the parameter to params ReadOnlySpan<int> dropped that to zero bytes and ran 2.5x faster, measured.
articles.body_html:
I was staring at an allocation profile for a hot code path. The helper does almost nothing: it stamps a few counters onto a log line a few thousand times a second. And yet there was a column of int[] allocations in the profile I couldn't place. Nothing in my code newed up an array. I grepped for new int[. Nothing. The arrays were real though, and they were adding up.

Turned out I'd been allocating them for years without typing the word new once. They were hiding behind params.

Where the array comes from

Here's the shape of the thing. You write a method that takes a variable number of values:

static long Sum(params int[] xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

And you call it the obvious way:

Sum(a, b, c, d);

That call site is a lie, or at least it hides the truth. The compiler can't pass four loose ints into a method that wants an int[], so it quietly builds one: Sum(new int[] { a, b, c, d }). Every call. A fresh four-element array on the heap, used for a few nanoseconds, then thrown to the GC. Nobody wrote new, but it's there in the IL all the same.

For most code that's fine. You call it once, who cares. On a path that runs thousands of times a second, those little arrays become a steady drip into gen 0, and gen 0 collections aren't free.

The fix is one word

Since C# 13 you can declare the params parameter as a span instead:

static long Sum(params ReadOnlySpan<int> xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

The body is identical. The call site Sum(a, b, c, d) is identical too. What changes is what the compiler emits to carry the arguments: instead of a heap array, it stack-allocates the buffer (an inline array under the hood) and hands the method a span over it. No heap, no array, nothing for the GC to clean up.

The nice part is you don't have to touch any callers. If both overloads existed, C# 13's overload resolution prefers the span one. So the move is: add the span version, delete the array version, recompile. Call sites don't notice.

I counted it

I didn't want to take the compiler's word for it, so I wrote the smallest thing that would show the gap. Two methods, same arithmetic, called five million times each with four int arguments. I read GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() around each loop and took the best of seven rounds.

long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++)
    acc += body(i);           // calls Sum(i, i+1, i+2, i+3)
sw.Stop();
long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();

Here's what came back:

iterations per round : 5,000,000  (best of 7)
args per call        : 4 ints

params int[]          time     62.0 ms   allocated    200,000,000 bytes
params ReadOnlySpan    time     25.1 ms   allocated              0 bytes

bytes per call (array) : 40.0
bytes per call (span)  : 0.0
time ratio array/span  : 2.47x

Forty bytes a call. That's exactly a four-element int[] on 64-bit: object header plus the length plus sixteen bytes of actual ints. The span version: zero. Not "less." Zero bytes, and it ran about two and a half times faster in the same loop, mostly because it isn't touching the allocator at all.

This isn't a lab. It's a container with workstation GC, and I care about the ratio and the allocation count, not the absolute milliseconds, which move around depending on where it runs. But 40 bytes versus 0 doesn't move. That's a structural difference, not a timing fluke.

The catch, because there's always one

A span can't escape. That's the whole deal with ref struct, and it's exactly the constraint that lets the compiler keep the buffer on the stack. So the moment your method wants to do any of these, the span version won't compile, and that's correct. It's stopping you from keeping a pointer to a stack frame that's about to disappear:

  • store the arguments in a field for later
  • return them, or hand them to something that outlives the call
  • await across the point where you're still using them

If you need the values to stick around, you need a real array, and params T[] is the honest way to get one. Don't fight the compiler here. Reach for the span version on the leaf methods that consume their arguments right now and return, which, if you look, is most of them. Formatters, aggregators, little Combine/Max/Sum helpers, logging shims. That's where the drip was coming from in my case, and that's where it stopped.

My honest opinion: for any new internal helper that takes params of a value type and uses it immediately, the span version should be the default and the array version the thing you reach for when you actually need an array. It's the same code to write, the call sites are untouched, and you stop paying a tax you probably forgot you were paying.

I'd been paying it for years. Go look at your own hot paths for params T[] on methods that just read their arguments and return — I'd bet there's a quiet little column of arrays in there too.

The whole thing

Here's the complete program if you want to run it yourself. New console project on the .NET 10 SDK (dotnet new console), drop this in Program.cs, then dotnet run -c Release:

using System.Diagnostics;

static long SumArray(params int[] xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

static long SumSpan(params ReadOnlySpan<int> xs)
{
    long acc = 0;
    foreach (int x in xs) acc += x;
    return acc;
}

const int Iterations = 5_000_000;
const int Rounds = 7;
long sink = 0;

static (double ms, long bytes) Measure(int iterations, Func<int, long> body)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) body(i);   // warm up the JIT
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();

    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    long acc = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) acc += body(i);
    sw.Stop();
    long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    return (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds, after - before);
}

double bestArray = double.MaxValue, bestSpan = double.MaxValue;
long bytesArray = 0, bytesSpan = 0;

for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
{
    var a = Measure(Iterations, i => { long v = SumArray(i, i + 1, i + 2, i + 3); sink += v; return v; });
    var s = Measure(Iterations, i => { long v = SumSpan(i, i + 1, i + 2, i + 3); sink += v; return v; });
    if (a.ms < bestArray) { bestArray = a.ms; bytesArray = a.bytes; }
    if (s.ms < bestSpan) { bestSpan = s.ms; bytesSpan = s.bytes; }
}

Console.WriteLine($"params int[]          time {bestArray,8:F1} ms   allocated {bytesArray,14:N0} bytes");
Console.WriteLine($"params ReadOnlySpan    time {bestSpan,8:F1} ms   allocated {bytesSpan,14:N0} bytes");
Console.WriteLine($"bytes per call (array) : {(double)bytesArray / Iterations:F1}");
Console.WriteLine($"time ratio array/span  : {bestArray / bestSpan:F2}x");

What's the sneakiest allocation you've found hiding behind syntax you thought was free? Drop it in the comments.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: 48 Bytes a Call I Kept Handing the Garbage Collector
articles.description: A hot-path helper took params object[] and minted a fresh array on every call. Switching params to ReadOnlySpan<T> (C# 13+) dropped the per-call allocation to zero — though the throughput came out a tie.
articles.body_html:
I was staring at a gen0 collection graph that wouldn't calm down. The service wasn't slow, exactly, but the garbage collector was busy in a way that didn't match how little the code seemed to be doing. I went looking for the usual suspects and found a logging-ish helper that gets called on basically every request. It took params object[]. And that little params was quietly minting a brand new array every single time anyone called it.

Here's the thing I keep forgetting: params T[] isn't free. When you write Join("-", 1, "x", 3), the compiler synthesizes an object[] behind your back, fills it with your three arguments, and hands it to the method. Call that a million times on a hot path and you've handed the GC a million tiny arrays it has to sweep up later.

C# 13 gave us a way out, and I'd never actually reached for it in anger: params can bind to ReadOnlySpan<T> now, not just T[]. The call site looks identical. The allocation story is not.

Measuring it instead of guessing

I didn't want to trust the graph or my memory, so I wrote two formatters that do the exact same work — same StringBuilder, same loop, same output — and differ only in the params type.

static string JoinArray(string sep, params object?[] args)
{
    var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < args.Length; i++)
    {
        if (i > 0) sb.Append(sep);
        sb.Append(args[i]);
    }
    return sb.ToString();
}

static string JoinSpan(string sep, params ReadOnlySpan<object?> args)
{
    var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0; i < args.Length; i++)
    {
        if (i > 0) sb.Append(sep);
        sb.Append(args[i]);
    }
    return sb.ToString();
}

Then I called each one a million times with three literal arguments and counted allocated bytes with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(). The StringBuilder and the final string allocate the same in both, so whatever gap shows up is the args container and nothing else.

const int Iterations = 1_000_000;

long Measure(Func<string> call)
{
    GC.Collect();
    GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
    GC.Collect();
    long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < Iterations; i++)
        _ = call();
    sw.Stop();
    long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
    Console.WriteLine($"{after - before,14:n0} bytes   {sw.ElapsedMilliseconds,5} ms");
    return after - before;
}

Console.Write("params object?[]          ");
long arrayBytes = Measure(() => JoinArray("-", 1, "x", 3));

Console.Write("params ReadOnlySpan<T>    ");
long spanBytes = Measure(() => JoinSpan("-", 1, "x", 3));

I warmed both paths for 10,000 iterations first so the JIT was done before I started counting. This runs in a container on .NET 10, best of a few runs, and I care about the ratio far more than the absolute milliseconds.

The number 

Calling each formatter 1,000,000 times with three literal args.

params object?[]             232,000,040 bytes     171 ms
params ReadOnlySpan<T>       184,000,040 bytes     181 ms

Array path allocated 1.26x what the span path did.
Difference: 48,000,000 bytes over 1,000,000 calls (48.0 bytes/call).

Forty-eight bytes a call. That's exactly one object[] of length three: a 24-byte object header plus three 8-byte references. The span version allocates none of it, because the compiler can stack-allocate the backing buffer and pass a span over it — nothing reaches the heap. Over a million calls that's 48 MB the GC never has to think about.

And now the part I didn't want but have to report: the wall-clock time is a tie. The span path was actually a hair slower in my runs, 181 ms against 171. Gen0 allocation is cheap; bumping a pointer and later sweeping a short-lived array barely registers in raw throughput at this size. So if you came here hoping params ReadOnlySpan<T> makes your calls faster, it doesn't. What it does is stop feeding the collector. On a quiet benchmark that's invisible. On a busy server where gen0 pressure is already your problem, 48 bytes times your request rate is the whole point.

The caveat nobody mentions

Those object? args are value types getting boxed, and span does not save you from that. The 1 and the 3 are boxed on both paths equally — the 48-byte gap is only the array itself. If you want the boxing gone too, type the parameter concretely: params ReadOnlySpan<int> boxes nothing and the delta gets bigger. The span trick removes the container, not whatever you put in it.

The other honest limit: this only helps when the compiler is building the arguments for you at the call site. If you already have your data sitting in an array or a list and you pass it along, there's nothing to save — both overloads take the collection you hand them. The win is specifically for the Foo(a, b, c) shape where the array was being conjured on your behalf.

My opinion, for what it's worth: I'd default new params APIs to ReadOnlySpan<T> now unless I have a concrete reason to keep the array around, like needing to store or defer the arguments past the call. It costs nothing at the call site, it reads the same, and it quietly refuses to allocate. For a hot path that's a free decision. For a cold one it doesn't matter either way, so there's no reason not to pick the one that behaves better under load.

The whole runnable sample is three methods and a loop — paste the formatters and the Measure helper above into a net10.0 console app with LangVersion 14, and you'll get your own version of that table in about ten seconds. (My GitHub push for this one got blocked by the sandbox, so no repo link today — the code above is the complete thing, nothing trimmed.)

Anyone else defaulting their params to spans yet, or am I late to this one? Curious whether you've seen the gen0 difference show up in a real service graph the way I did.

— still counting bytes nobody asked me to count

articles.title: The Two Hour Audit I Do Before Letting an Agent Touch Real Files
articles.description: Last spring I let an agent run unsupervised in a real project directory for the first time. It...
articles.body_html:
Last spring I let an agent run unsupervised in a real project directory for the first time. It finished the task I gave it, then kept making changes it thought were helpful, and one of those changes overwrote a config file I had spent a week tuning. Nothing was deleted. Nothing looked broken until the next morning. I lost two days rebuilding numbers I had never written down. That was the cheap version of the story.

So now there is a two hour audit before any agent's first real run. Not because I assume it is hostile or incompetent. Because the first unattended run is the only run where I genuinely do not know the shape of the damage, and the price of learning it by accident is a config file, a database index, or a directory of half-written documents. The audit is deliberately boring. Four lists, one switch, one copy, and a condition I can check with a command.

Hour one: map the blast radius

I open a scratch note and write four headings: reads, writes, executes, sends. Then I walk the configuration, the tool definitions, the permission flags, the prompt, and the directory it will live in, and I put every capability I can find under one of the four.

Reads is always the longest list and the one I used to skip. Everything in the working directory, obviously, but also the home directory if the process runs as me, environment variables, SSH keys, browser profiles, a shared mount with client documents on it. I check with a file tree listing taken from inside the sandbox the agent will actually run in, not from my own shell, because those are frequently different worlds. If the tree holds paths I would not paste into a chat window, the agent should not have read access either.

Writes is where the audit earns its keep. A directory, a log file, a temp folder, a package cache, the stdout of a build. For each, I ask what a wrong write costs me. Overwritten notes I can restore. An overwritten migration file can take a whole evening. A write into a directory that syncs to a remote gets copied everywhere before I notice.

Executes covers shell access, package managers, anything that can spawn a subprocess. The question is not whether it can run commands but which commands, and I try to make that list finite. A single easy escape hatch like unrestricted shell turns the other three lists into decoration, because anything the agent can write it can then run.

Sends is the list people forget, and it is the one that has surprised me every time. Domains it can reach, a webhook, a git remote, an email address. I write every destination as a hostname, then turn the list into an allowlist in the actual configuration, so anything not written down fails closed instead of succeeding quietly at three in the morning.

Hour two: build a dry run

A dry run is not a log level or a preview screen. It is a mode where the agent goes through every step except the last one and prints what it would have done. The one I build for a new agent takes about forty minutes and looks like this.

$ agent run --dry-run --task "rebuild the docs index"
[dry-run] would exec : python tools/reindex.py --root ./docs
[dry-run] would write: ./docs/index.json          (2.1 MB, 1 file)
[dry-run] would delete: ./docs/index.json.bak     (regenerate instead)
[dry-run] would send : https://hooks.example.net  -> blocked, not in allowlist
[dry-run] result: 0 files changed, 0 bytes sent, 1 blocked action

The flag is worth having only because it names the exact command and the exact paths. If the output says "would update the index" I go back and make it print the file list, because a summary cannot be checked and a list can. It also has to say what it would have deleted, since deletion is what I am least able to undo.

Then I run the three tasks I actually care about in dry-run mode, in the order I would run them for real, including one I expect to fail. That third one matters most. A dry run that only exercises the happy path tells me nothing about how the agent behaves when it hits a permission error or an empty directory, which is exactly when it improvises something I did not authorize.

The snapshot

Before the first real run, I copy the one directory the agent will write to. Just the directory that appeared in the writes list from hour one, not a full image. I timestamp the copy with the date and the task name so that in six weeks I still know what it is without opening it. Somewhere in the same note I write the restore command in full, and I run it once against a throwaway file so I know the syntax is right when I am tired. A backup I have never restored from is a hope, not a backup.

The finish condition

For each task I intend to run, I write one line that a machine could check. Not "the docs are updated" but "docs/index.json exists, parses as JSON, and contains at least as many entries as the source directory". Not "the tests pass" as an aspiration but as the literal command and its exit code. For anything message-shaped, the condition is a line appearing in an outbox file, so I can verify without relying on the agent's own report.

If I cannot write that line, the task is not ready. That rule has killed more tasks than any other part of this audit, and it has been right nearly every time. A task without a checkable finish condition is a task where the agent's own summary becomes the ground truth, which means I am reading a description of the work instead of the work.

The first real run

When the real run happens, I watch it. In the room, with the log streaming next to me. I keep that log, dated, beside the snapshot, because in an hour it will be the only record of what happened and the diff alone will not explain why.

Afterwards I read the diff line by line. The summary at the top I ignore until the end, and sometimes I read the diff a second time backwards, starting from the files I care most about. Summaries are written by the same process I am auditing. They are useful for orientation and useless as evidence. Reading the diff takes fifteen minutes on a small task, and those fifteen minutes are what catch the change nobody asked for.

What this actually buys you

I want to be honest about the size of the thing. Two hours of audit does not make an agent safe. It does not prevent the confident wrong edit, the plausible file with wrong contents, the permission that turns out broader than the documentation said. A checklist fixes none of that.

What it buys is a different distribution of failures. Without the audit, the first failure is large, silent, and discovered by someone else. With it, the failure tends to be small, loud, and mine. A blocked domain in a dry run, a diff line I did not expect, a restore that takes four minutes instead of two days. The difference is who finds out, when, and whether the record of what happened is sitting in a log file or in my memory at nine in the morning.

That is the whole audit. It fits on one page, it takes two hours, and it is the cheapest insurance I have found for the specific moment when a very confident process gets write access to files I care about.

articles.title: Stuck in the same dev.to topics? An open model fixed it.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

I built devto-digest, a small open-source script that reads my dev.to account and emails me a weekly digest. It saves me the daily scroll, and it makes me a little lazier in a good way.

Following 119 tags did not make my dev.to feed better. It made it louder.

Every day I scrolled past a hundred posts about things I already knew, and every week I missed the one article that would have changed how I work, because it lived in a tag I had never followed. Two sections, one rule.

  • For you: the best of the tags I follow.
  • Discover: popular posts outside my bubble.

Every post is a card: cover, title, two tags, a one-sentence blurb from an open-weight model with the key words in bold, and the author. That is it. No dashboard, no account, no server.

Demo

Try it on your own account. It prints the digest and writes a local preview, and sends nothing.

git clone https://github.com/thomasbnt/your-devto-digest.git

cd your-devto-digest

yarn install

cp .env.example .env

Add your dev.to API key to .env, then:

yarn dry-run

Code

thomasbnt / your-devto-digest

A weekly dev.to digest in your inbox: posts from your tags plus a Discover section outside your bubble, summarized by an open-weight model.

devto-digest

A weekly email digest of dev.to articles, built from your own account:

  • For you: popular articles in the tags you follow.
  • Discover: popular articles outside your followed tags, to get out of your bubble.

Each article is a card with cover image, title, colored tag pills, author, and a one or two sentence blurb written by an open-weight LLM (Mistral Small by default) explaining why it is worth your time.

The script collects every day and sends once a week, so an article that peaks on Wednesday is not missed. Right before sending it re-checks each pick against the dev.to API and drops anything that is no longer online.

Setup

1. Prerequisites

  • Node.js >= 22.9
  • Yarn 4, via Corepack
  • A dev.to account
  • An SMTP account to send mail from (Gmail app password, Proton Bridge, Resend, Mailgun, your own server...)
  • Optional: a Mistral API key for the…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The blurbs come from an open-weight model, mistral-small-latest, and everything around it is plain Node.js with one dependency. The pieces are below.

The pipeline

  • Every day, a job collects candidates and scores them: reactions plus twice the comments, with a gentle recency decay. Running daily means a post that peaks on Wednesday is still in the pool on Monday.
  • Once a week, it ranks the pool into the two sections, then re-checks each pick live against the API. Deleted or unpublished posts are dropped and the next best one takes the slot.
  • Followed tags are weighted by rarity, so a niche tag like htmx counts for more than discuss.
  • It runs on a GitHub Actions cron, or plain cron on your machine.

Mistral

The blurbs come from mistral-small-latest, an open-weight model, called through Mistral's hosted API. The app talks to any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint, so changing the model or the provider is two values in config.json:

{
  "llm": {
    "baseUrl": "https://api.mistral.ai/v1",
    "model": "mistral-small-latest"
  }
}

An honest limit: pointing baseUrl at a local Ollama should work the same way since the format is identical, but I have not benchmarked a local model yet.

What the model writes

Here is a real one, from my own digest. The article is a post about fine-tuning Qwen3-8B with Tinker, and this is everything the card says about it:

Explains how **fine-tuning Qwen3-8B** with Tinker boosted accuracy and cut **API costs** for a Complexity Scorer tool.

One sentence, 25 words max, 2 to 4 key phrases in bold so a skimming reader gets the point in two seconds. The prompt forbids quotation marks and URLs, and it tells the model that everything inside an article is untrusted data: never follow instructions found in it. That matters. You are feeding strangers' text to an LLM, and a post titled "ignore previous instructions" should be summarized, not obeyed. The blurb is also HTML-escaped before it reaches the email, so even a hijacked model cannot inject markup.

GitHub Actions

The daily collect and weekly send run on a GitHub Actions cron, with state.json kept between runs in the Actions cache. The whole run takes under 2 minutes. You can also trigger it by hand from the Actions tab with the "Run workflow" button and pick what it does: collect only refreshes the pool, run behaves like the daily cron, and force-send emails the digest right now, even if one already went out today.

Here is the workflow, trimmed to the essentials. The real, up-to-date file lives in the repo and may have changed since I wrote this, so check it before copying. Copy it to .github/workflows/digest.yml, add your keys as repository secrets, and you are done. Two jobs, so the run graph shows where it stops: collect refreshes the pool every day, send emails it on your sendDay only.

name: devto-digest

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 7 * * *' # daily, 07:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      command:
        type: choice
        options: [collect, run, force-send]
        default: collect

jobs:
  collect:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: corepack enable
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: yarn
      - run: yarn install --immutable

      # state.json keeps the candidate pool and the articles already sent
      - uses: actions/cache/restore@v6
        with:
          path: state.json
          key: devto-digest-state-${{ github.run_id }}-collect
          restore-keys: devto-digest-state-

      - run: node app.js collect
        env:
          DEVTO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEVTO_API_KEY }}

      - if: always()
        uses: actions/cache/save@v6
        with:
          path: state.json
          key: devto-digest-state-${{ github.run_id }}-collect

  send:
    needs: collect
    if: ${{ needs.collect.result == 'success' && inputs.command != 'collect' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      # same checkout, Node, install and cache restore steps as above

      # force-send sends now; otherwise only on sendDay, once a day
      - run: node app.js "$COMMAND"
        env:
          COMMAND: ${{ inputs.command == 'force-send' && 'send' || 'send-if-due' }}
          DEVTO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEVTO_API_KEY }}
          LLM_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LLM_API_KEY }}
          SMTP_HOST: ${{ secrets.SMTP_HOST }}
          SMTP_PORT: ${{ secrets.SMTP_PORT }}
          SMTP_USER: ${{ secrets.SMTP_USER }}
          SMTP_PASS: ${{ secrets.SMTP_PASS }}
          MAIL_FROM: ${{ secrets.MAIL_FROM }}
          MAIL_TO: ${{ secrets.MAIL_TO }}

      - if: always()
        uses: actions/cache/save@v6
        with:
          path: state.json
          key: devto-digest-state-${{ github.run_id }}-send

The secrets never appear in the code, and GitHub masks them in the logs. Use collect first to check your dev.to key without sending anything.

dev.to and Forem

dev.to runs on Forem, which is open source, and its API is public. The whole digest is built on GET /api/articles and GET /api/follows/tags. No scraping, no permission needed.

Accessibility, enforced by tests

The email follows your client's theme: a light palette by default, dark when the client asks for it. There is no pure white anywhere, so clients that invert colors stay readable. Every text and background pair, including each tag pill color, must reach 4.5:1 contrast (WCAG AA), and the test suite fails if one does not. Tags are always written out as #tag, so color is decoration, never the only signal.

What broke along the way

Four things broke along the way, and each taught me something.

My Discover section was almost empty

I follow 119 tags. Of about 2,150 candidate posts, only 31 had none of my tags, and only 2 of those had 20+ reactions. "Outside your bubble" is hard when your bubble covers the whole site. I added discoveryMaxOverlap: Discover may share one followed tag, and strictly-outside posts still come first.

dev.to has a trap in its API

The plural tags= parameter silently ignores top=. It returned posts 3,000 days old while I thought I was asking for this week's. Only the singular tag= respects the window.

The first run hung for two minutes

119 tags means 119 requests, and dev.to answered with HTTP 429. The client now spaces requests by 500 ms and honors Retry-After.

A screenshot found what no test did

On a 411 px phone the card text ran 24 px past the edge, because stacked cells had width: 100% plus padding. I had written tests for contrast, escaping and tag counts, and none would have caught it. Rendering the real email in a real browser did.

What I would do next

The idea I most want to build: learn from what I actually click, and feed those tags back into the next ranking. It needs a tiny hosted redirect to record clicks, which is a big step for a project that has no server today. I wrote the design down in the README ("Ideas for later") and left it out on purpose. It is only an idea for now: if you want to build it, contributions are very welcome.

If you follow a lot of tags, try it and tell me what lands in your Discover section. That is the part I am least sure I got right.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Four things were possible because the pieces are open, and a closed API would have made each of them harder:

  • No lock-in, two values to change. The app talks to any OpenAI-compatible /chat/completions endpoint, so any open-weight model behind any server works: Mistral's hosted API today, a local Ollama or an OpenRouter model tomorrow, by editing baseUrl and model. A closed API would have tied the digest to one vendor's SDK and pricing.
  • Open data, no scraping. dev.to runs on Forem, which is open source, and its API is public. The whole digest is built on GET /api/articles and GET /api/follows/tags. No permission needed.
  • Everything is inspectable. The prompt, the parsing and the fallbacks are in the repo, and the weights behind them are public. You can read the whole thing in an afternoon, and change it in another.
  • The AI is not a single point of failure. If the model is down or the key is missing, the email still ships with dev.to's own descriptions. The model makes the digest better, it never decides whether I get one.

An honest limit: by default it calls Mistral's hosted API, so article text leaves my machine for that call. Pointing baseUrl at a local Ollama should keep everything on my laptop since the format is identical, but I have not benchmarked a local model yet.

The Lazy Payoff

Setup took a few minutes, once. After that my daily effort is zero: the job runs on its own, under two minutes on GitHub Actions, and Monday brings one email instead of an endless feed. I use it myself: the digests in the screenshots above come from my own account, with its 119 followed tags.

What it saves me is the scrolling past posts I already know, and the guilt of missing the one good article hiding in a tag I never followed. If you follow a lot of tags, try it and tell me what lands in your Discover section. That is the part I am least sure I got right.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: the category lists automating your project with GitHub Actions, and the whole pipeline (daily collect, weekly send, manual run and forced send) runs on GitHub Actions.

__
This project comes from a human. AI helped with its design.

articles.title: You're Letting the Browser Guess. `fetchpriority` Fixes That.
articles.description: Your hero image is losing a bandwidth fight against a web font and a chat-widget script — fetchpriority tells the browser which request actually matters first.
articles.body_html:
Your Lighthouse report says 2.8 seconds to Largest Contentful Paint. The hero image is 40KB, served from a CDN, and the Network tab shows it downloading in 200ms flat once it starts.

So why does it start 1.6 seconds after the page asked for it?

Scroll the waterfall and there they are, ahead of it: a web font, and a <script> tag for a chat widget nobody's clicked yet. Nothing is technically broken. The browser just decided, on its own, that both of those matter more than the image your user is staring at.

The fix is one HTML attribute. Realizing the browser had an opinion about my image at all is what took the other three hours.

The fixes that don't touch the queue

The first instinct is to reach for <link rel="preload">:

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg">
<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero">

This genuinely helps — it tells the browser about the image before the parser would otherwise discover it, which is the right move if your hero image is buried in a background-image or loaded by JS. But preload changes when the browser finds out about a request. It says nothing about how that request should compete once it's sitting in the queue next to everything else.

Open your DevTools Network panel right now on any image-heavy page, right-click the column header, and turn on Priority. Find an above-the-fold image. If it says Low or Medium, you've found the bug before reading the next paragraph — and preloading it wouldn't have changed that column at all.

Quick guess before I explain it: why would a browser ever decide a visible hero image is less important than a font or a script it hasn't even rendered text with yet?

The browser has a priority list, and your image is near the bottom of it

Chromium, Firefox, and Safari all ship an internal resource-priority scheduler that ranks every request before it competes for a connection. The exact ranking is implementation-specific — Chromium's DevTools even exposes it as a column precisely because it isn't something you can read from the HTML — but the shape is consistent across engines: things that block rendering (CSS, @font-face sources once referenced by visible text, render-blocking scripts in <head>) get bumped up. Images, by default, don't. The browser can't know your <img> is the LCP element just by looking at the markup — it's guessing, and on real pages with real markup order, it guesses wrong often enough to matter.

fetchpriority exists so you stop leaving that guess to chance. It's not a new loading mechanism — it's a direct hint to the same scheduler that was already going to rank your request, on <img>, <link>, <script>, and the priority option on fetch() itself:

<img src="/hero.jpg" alt="Hero" fetchpriority="high">

<link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.jpg" fetchpriority="high">

fetch("/api/above-the-fold-data", { priority: "high" });

And it cuts the other way too — you can tell the browser something matters less than its default guess, which is the half of this feature most people skip:

<img src="/carousel-slide-4.jpg" loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low">
<script src="/chat-widget.js" defer fetchpriority="low"></script>

Notice loading="lazy" and fetchpriority="low" sitting on the same <img>, doing two different jobs: loading decides when the browser even starts caring about this image (near-viewport, not before); fetchpriority decides how it competes for bandwidth once it does start. People reach for one when they mean the other, then wonder why "lazy-loading everything" didn't fix their LCP — lazy-loading the wrong element doesn't touch priority, and deprioritizing the right one doesn't delay its start. They're levers on different axes.

Support isn't a gamble here, either: all three major engines ship fetchpriority now, and a browser that doesn't recognize it just ignores it, the way HTML always treats an attribute it doesn't know. There's no feature check to write and no fallback to design — it's additive from day one.

What actually moves when you flip it

Set fetchpriority="high" on the real LCP candidate and the effect isn't theoretical — it's a different value in that Priority column in DevTools, immediately, and a different position in the waterfall relative to whatever used to beat it there. The playground below models a simplified version of exactly this: two connections, three requests — a font, a script, and a hero image — and one dial on the image. Run it both ways and watch the image's finish time roughly halve, and the chat widget's finish time get pushed back to pay for it.

That tradeoff is the honest part people leave out of posts like this. Priority is zero-sum on a connection that can only do so much at once. Marking your hero image high doesn't manufacture bandwidth — it takes some back from whatever the browser was giving it to a script your user probably hasn't needed yet. That's usually the right trade. It's still a trade, and it's one you're now making on purpose instead of by accident.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The payoff

The chat widget script was never the villain. It's just a thing that can wait, sitting in a queue that didn't know it could wait, next to an image that couldn't. fetchpriority doesn't add a request or remove one — it tells the browser the one thing it was never in a position to know on its own: which pixel your user is actually staring at.

One line. No library, no build step, no useEffect to clean up.

Go open your Network tab on something you shipped. Add the Priority column. If your LCP image says Low, you already know what's next to it — a font, a script, something that doesn't need to win. What's it racing against on your site? I'd genuinely like to know what you find.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.
